figure_inventory.description: Start of a two-column hanging-indent list (power of ten in the left margin column, the fact in the right text column; no ruled lines, no colour). One entry on this page: left '10^0' (written 100 with the exponent raised); right: 'As of mid-2025, there are only two northern white rhinos remaining in the world, both females, and they reside at the Ol Pejeta Conservancy in Kenya (= 2 × 10^0).' The list continues on the next page (entries 10^1 to 10^9). The intro text before it names lakh = 10^5, crore = 10^7, arab = 10^9, million = 10^6, billion = 10^9 (printed in the text, not in the list).

Two-column hanging-indent list continued (power of ten in the left margin column; fact text on the right; no rules, no colour), 9 entries in this order: 10^1: As of early 2024 the total population of Hainan gibbons is a meagre 42 (≈ 4 × 10^1). 10^2: There are just 242 Kakapo alive as of mid-2025 (≈ 2 × 10^2). 10^3: fewer than 3000 Komodo dragons in the world, all based in Indonesia (≈ 3 × 10^3). 10^4: A 2005 estimate of the maned wolf population showed more than 17000 of them; most are in Brazil (1.7 × 10^4). [a strip of 5 stamp photographs is printed here: white rhinoceros $500 Liberia, Hainan gibbon 80 China, maned wolf RPKampuchea, Kakapo 30c New Zealand, Komodo dragon 300 Republik Indonesia - decorative photographs, not listed separately] 10^5: As of 2018, around 4.15 lakh African elephants (≈ 4 × 10^5). 10^6: an estimated 50 lakh / 5 million American alligators as of 2025 (5 × 10^6). 10^7: global camel population over 3.5 crore / 35 million (3.5 × 10^7), India only about 2.5 lakhs of them; global horse population around 5.8 crore / 58 million (5.8 × 10^7), about half of them in America. 10^8: More than 20 crore / 200 million (2 × 10^8) water buffaloes worldwide, a vast majority in Asia. 10^9: estimated global population of starlings around 1.3 arab / 1.3 billion (a BLANK bracket '( ________ )' for the student to write in scientific notation); the global human population as of 2025 is 8.2 arab / 8.2 billion (8.2 × 10^9). Below the list: a full-width photograph of a starling murmuration over a farm in the UK with the caption 'A picture of a starling murmuration over a farm in the UK. Starling murmuration is a mesmerising aerial display of thousands of starlings flying in synchronised, swirling patterns. It is often described as a choreographed dance.' (photograph, not worked on).

Two-column hanging-indent list continued (power in the left margin column; fact text on the right; no rules, no colour). Before it, the boxed-question line: 'With a global human population of about 8 × 10^9 and about 4 × 10^5 African elephants, can we say that there are nearly 20,000 people for every African elephant?'. 8 entries in this order: 10^10: global chicken population living at any time ≈ 33 billion (3.3 × 10^10). 10^12: estimated number of trees (2023) globally 30 kharab / 3 trillion (3 × 10^12); one kharab is 100 arab, one trillion is 1000 billion. 10^14: estimated mosquito population worldwide (2023) 11 neel / 110 trillion (a BLANK bracket '( ________ )' for the student); derived estimate of the Antarctic krill population 50 neel / 500 trillion (5 × 10^14). 10^15: beetle population estimate 1 padma / 1 quadrillion (1 × 10^15); earthworm population also 1 padma / 1 quadrillion. 10^16: estimated ant population 20 padma / 20 quadrillion (2 × 10^16); 'Ants alone outweigh all wild birds and wild mammals combined.' 10^21 (this entry is a normal full-width paragraph, the '10^21' is the first word, not in the margin): supposed number of grains of sand on all beaches and deserts on Earth; 'enough sand to give every ant 10 little sand castles to live in.' 10^23: estimated number of stars in the observable universe is 2 × 10^23. 10^25: an estimated 2 × 10^25 drops of water on Earth (assuming 16 drops per millilitre). Illustrations beside/inside it (decorative, not listed separately): a krill picture, the balance picture (listed as P20-balance-1) and a wide picture of sand castles with one small ant at the right end.

Colour illustration of a two-pan balance (weighing scale), no numbers or labels. The beam is tilted: its left end is low, its right end high. LEFT pan (small round dish hanging from the beam by three strings) holds a black heap of ants. RIGHT pan (a dark boat-shaped tray hanging from the right end of the beam on two rods) is crowded with wild animals and birds (an elephant, giraffe, gorilla, deer, lion, tiger, monkey, peacock and other birds). The left (ants) pan hangs lower than the right (animals) pan, i.e. the ants side is the heavier. A thin horizontal line and a vertical line frame the upper right of the scale as part of the stand. [Checked against the page picture: qualitative picture of ants against wild animals, no numbers, no question uses it.]

Colour comic panel: a pink rounded panel with Estu (boy, teal shirt, arms crossed, small figure at left) and Roxie (girl, curly hair in two puffs, yellow top, smiling, pointing at Estu). A white speech bubble comes from Roxie with the text on three lines: 'I am' / '69,70,710 ...' / 'old'. Caption printed under the panel on two lines: 'What could this number mean?' / 'Find out!'. The only mathematical content is the number text in the bubble. [Checked against the page picture: the digits read 69,70,710 in one size, plain digits, no raised exponents; the same number is in the LP question text of M6.S28.T28.C136 (6970710).]

Two-column table, first part. Header: a pink band across the full width with the bold titles 'Time in seconds' (left column) and 'Comparison to real-world events/phenomena' (right column), a thin dark rule under the header. Body rows have no ruled lines and no colour; the right column items start with a '-' dash. Rows on this page: (1) '10^0 = 1 second' | '- Time taken for a ball thrown up to fall back on the ground (typically a few seconds).' (2) '10^1 = 10 seconds' | '- Time blood takes to complete one full circulation through the body: 10–20 seconds (1 × 10^1 – 2 × 10^1 seconds).' and '- Typical waiting time at a traffic signal.' (3) after the blue owl text box 'Isn't it quite amazing how someone is able to estimate things like the number of ants in the world or the time blood takes to fully circulate?...' interrupts the table: '10^2 seconds ≈1.6 minutes' | '- Time needed to make a cup of tea: 5–10 minutes (≈ 4 × 10^2 – 8 × 10^2 seconds).' and '- Time for light to reach the Earth from the Sun: about 8 minutes (≈ 5 × 10^2 seconds).' Rows 1 and 2 give '= 1 second' / '= 10 seconds'; row 3 gives only '≈1.6 minutes'. 3 rows, 5 bulleted comparisons on this page. The table continues on p.22 without a repeated header.

Two-column table continued (no header band repeated, no ruled lines, no colour, dash bullets in the right column), 5 rows: (1) '10^3 seconds ≈ 16.6 minutes' | '- Satellites in low Earth orbits take between 90 minutes (≈ 5.5 × 10^3 seconds) to 2 hours to complete one full revolution around the Earth.' (2) '10^4 seconds ≈ 2.7 hours' | '- The time needed to digest a meal: about 2–4 hours to pass through the stomach.' and '- Lifespan of an adult mayfly: about a day (≈ 9 × 10^4 seconds).' [mayfly illustration at the right]. Then the printed question breaks the table (rows 10^5 and 10^6 are NOT in the table): '10^5 seconds ≈ 1.16 days and 10^6 seconds ≈ 11.57 days. Think of some events or phenomena whose time is of the order of (i) 10^5 seconds and (ii) 10^6 seconds. Write them in scientific notation.' (3) '10^7 seconds ≈ 115.7 days / ≈ 3.8 months' | '- Time spent sleeping in a year: about 4 months.', '- Time taken by Mangalyaan mission to reach Mars: 298 days (≈ 2.65 × 10^7 seconds).', '- Time taken by Mars for one full revolution around the Sun: 687 Earth-days/1.88 Earth-years (≈ 6 × 10^7 seconds).' [Mangalyaan picture at the right] (4) '10^8 seconds ≈ 3.17 years' | '- The typical lifespan of most dogs is 3 to 15 years.' (5) '10^9 seconds ≈ 31.7 years' | '- The orbital period of Halley's comet is 75–79 years; the next expected return is in the year 2061 (≈ 2.4 × 10^9 seconds).' and '- Duration of one full revolution of Neptune around the Sun: 60,190 Earth-days/~165 Earth-years or 89,666 Neptunian days/1 Neptunian-year (≈ 5.2 × 10^9 seconds). A day on Neptune is about 16.1 hours'. 5 rows, 9 bulleted comparisons. At the top of the page a 3-panel comic (Roxie with a noodle packet 'These liars!! It never gets cooked before 10 minutes...', Estu 'They should approximate it as order of 10^2 seconds noodles - that way whether it takes 120 seconds or 900 seconds, the claim will be true.', both laughing) - dialogue picture, decorative.

Two-column table continued (no header band, no ruled lines, no colour, dash bullets in the right column), 6 rows, 10 bulleted comparisons. Text above the table: 'Notice how rapid exponential growth is - 10^6 seconds is less than a fortnight, but 10^9 seconds is a whopping 31 years (about half the life expectancy of a human)!' Rows: (1) '10^10 seconds ≈ 317 years' | '- The Chola dynasty ruled for more than 900 years (≈ 3 × 10^10 seconds) between the 3rd Century BCE and 12th Century CE.' (2) '10^11 seconds ≈ 3,170 years' | '- Age of the oldest known living tree: about 5000 years (≈ 1.57 × 10^11 seconds).' and '- Time since the last peak ice age: 19,000 – 26,000 years ago (≈ 6 × 10^11 seconds – 8.2 × 10^11 seconds).' (3) '10^12 seconds ≈ 31,700 years' | '- Early Homo sapiens first appeared 2–3 lakh years ago (≈ 7 × 10^12 – 9 × 10^12 seconds). The entire population around that time could fit in a large cricket stadium.' (4) '10^13 seconds ≈ 3.17 lakh years' | '- The Steppe Mammoth is estimated to have appeared around 8–18 lakh years ago.' [mammoth illustration at the right] (5) '10^14 seconds ≈ 3.17 million years' | '- A fossil of Kelenken Guillermoi, a type of terror bird, is dated to 15 million years ago (≈ ______________ seconds).' - a BLANK for the student; [terror-bird illustration at the right] (6) '10^15 seconds ≈ 3.17 crore years' | '- Age of Himalayas: 5.5 crore years/55 million years (≈ 1.7 × 10^15 seconds); they continue to grow a few mm every year.', '- Dinosaurs went extinct 6.6 crore years ago/66 million years ago (≈ 2 × 10^15 seconds).', '- Dinosaurs first appeared more than 20 crore/200 million years ago (≈ 6 × 10^15 seconds).', '- It takes about 23 crore years for the Sun to make one complete trip around the Milky Way (≈ 7 × 10^15 seconds).'

Two-column table, last part (no header band, no ruled lines, no colour), 2 rows, 4 comparisons. (1) '10^16 seconds ≈ 31.7 crore years' | '- Plants on land started 47 crore/470 million years ago (≈ ______________ seconds).' - a BLANK for the student. (2) '10^17 seconds ≈ 3.17 billion years' | 'The oldest fossil evidence suggests that bacteria first appeared about 3.7 billion years ago.' (this first line has no '-' dash printed), '- The Earth is 4.5 billion years old.', '- The Milky Way galaxy was formed 13.6 billion years ago, and the Universe was formed 13.8 billion years ago.' After the table: 'Notice that 10^9 seconds is of the order of the lifespan of a human, whereas 10^18 seconds ago the universe did not exist according to modern physics!!'

Three-column table with no ruled lines and no colour, centred text, 4 rows (no header row). Column 1 (words, two lines each) | column 2 (numerals) | column 3 (powers of 10): (1) 'A hundred thousand is a lakh' | '100 × 1000 = 1,00,000' | '10^2 × 10^3 = 10^5'. (2) 'A hundred lakhs is a crore' | '100 × 1,00,000 = 1,00,00,000' | '10^2 × 10^5 = 10^7'. (3) 'A hundred crores is an arab' | '100 × 1,00,00,000 = 1,00,00,00,000' | '10^2 × 10^7 = 10^9'. (4) 'A hundred arab is a kharab' | '100 × 1,00,00,00,000' on one line and '= 1,00,00,00,00,000' on a second line | '10^2 × 10^9 = 10^11'. Text after the table: a hundred kharab is a neel (10^13), a hundred neel a padma (10^15), a hundred padma a shankh (10^17), a hundred shankh a maha shankh (10^19). [Plain table; nothing is drawn from it. The concept image M6.S30.T30.C144.IMG1 is a separate staircase drawing of the same four names, so it is not claimed here.]

Three-column table, same style as the Indian-system table above (no ruled lines, no colour, centred text), 3 rows, no header row: (1) 'A thousand thousand is a million' | '1000 × 1000 = 1,000,000' | '10^3 × 10^3 = 10^6'. (2) 'A thousand million is a billion' | '1000 × 1,000,000 = 1,000,000,000' | '10^3 × 10^6 = 10^9'. (3) 'A thousand billion is a trillion' | '1000 × 1,000,000,000' on one line and '= 1,00,000,000,000' on a second line | '10^3 × 10^9 = 10^12'. Text after the table: a thousand trillion is a quadrillion (10^15); the names million (10^6), billion (10^9), trillion (10^12), quadrillion (10^15), quintillion (10^18), sextillion (10^21), septillion (10^24), octillion (10^27), nonillion (10^30), decillion (10^33) are printed with their first parts bold (mi, bi, tr, quad, quin, sext, sept, oct, non, dec) for the question 'What does the first part of each name denote?' items.ncert_ref: Section 2.5 - A Pinch of History (pp.24-25): Indian names lakh, crore, arab, kharab, neel

The book's own picture here is the plain three-column table on p.25 (words, numerals, powers; no colour), and the concept image M6.S30.T30.C144.IMG1 already shows the staircase; a teaching image is never linked, and the example does not need a figure of its own.
